summary:
Star Base is a free browser game (no download, no account) where kids aged 7–12 run a base on the Moon or Mars and keep 4 astronauts alive. Each day they share limited solar energy between life support (air), a greenhouse (food), a radiation shield and a science lab. Live green/red numbers show if each choice is enough, so trade-offs are felt instantly. Surprise events (solar storms, Martian dust storms, micrometeorites, ice discoveries) force real decisions, and the long lunar night rewards planning with the battery. Every 3 days players pick an upgrade, like a nuclear reactor, regolith shielding or a MOXIE-style oxygen maker. Two levels: Cadet (10 days, ages 7–9) and Commander (15 days, ages 10–12, families, classrooms). Up to 3 stars for survival, science and low radiation; failing means a safe trip home.

Grounded in real data: the radiation meter uses real millisieverts and ends at NASA’s 600 mSv career limit. Daily doses come from Curiosity’s RAD on Mars (0.64 mSv/day) and the Chang’e 4 lander on the Moon (1.37 mSv/day), sped up and clearly explained. A “Real data” panel charts these values with linked sources, and events tagged “Real data” cite actual missions. All data is curated and labeled as not live.

Accessible: plain language, tap-to-explain science terms, read-aloud, big buttons, keyboard support, and discussion questions for families and teachers.

details:
Star Base: Run Your Own Moon or Mars Outpost
Play: https://star-base-game-synaphi13-7493.vercel.app

What does it do and how does it work?
Star Base is a browser game for kids aged 7–12. Players run a small base on the Moon or Mars and keep four astronauts alive. Each day the solar panels produce a limited amount of energy, and the player shares it between four systems:

  • Life support, which makes air
  • The greenhouse, which grows food
  • The radiation shield
  • The science lab

Live green and red numbers show right away whether each choice keeps air, food and radiation in a safe range. Random events make players change their plans:

  • Solar storms
  • Martian dust storms
  • Micrometeorites
  • Finding ice
  • Cargo deliveries

Some events ask for a decision, like spending spacesuit air to explore a rock for extra science. The Moon’s long lunar night and Mars’ multi-day dust storms reward saving energy in a battery. Every three days players choose an upgrade, such as a nuclear reactor, regolith shielding or a MOXIE-style oxygen maker. There are two levels: Cadet (10 days, ages 7–9) and Commander (15 days, ages 10–12, families and classrooms). Players earn up to three stars for survival, science and low radiation. If a mission fails, the crew simply flies home safely.

What benefits does it have?

  • Learning by doing: instead of reading that space missions are hard, kids make the trade-offs themselves. Science or safety? Food now, or battery for the night?
  • Real science: the radiation meter uses real units (millisieverts) and ends at NASA’s real 600 mSv career limit for astronauts. Daily doses come from published measurements:
    A “Real data” panel charts these values with linked sources. Events tagged “Real data” describe actual missions, such as MOXIE, Opportunity and LCROSS.
    • Mars: Curiosity’s RAD instrument, 0.64 mSv/day
    • Moon: the Chang’e 4 lander, 1.37 mSv/day
  • Easy to reach: it runs in any browser on phones, tablets and computers, with no download, account or install.

What is the intended impact?
We want kids to feel what real mission planners face: limited resources, competing needs and uncertainty. We also want them to connect those choices to real NASA data. The end-of-game discussion questions turn one play session into a conversation at home or in class. That way the game sparks curiosity about space careers, engineering and science.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did we use?

  • Code: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript in one self-contained file, with no frameworks.
  • Graphics: the base scene is drawn in SVG and changes with the game. Panels appear, the greenhouse glows, the shield appears, and storms are animated.
  • Read-aloud: the browser’s built-in Web Speech API.
  • Fonts: Google Fonts (Baloo 2 and Nunito).
  • Hosting: Vercel.
  • Development help: we built the game with Claude, an AI assistant, which helped with coding, research and checking sources.
  • Testing: we ran automated playtests in a headless browser (Playwright) on every mode.
  • Data sources: peer-reviewed papers (Science, Science Advances), NASA technical standards and NASA mission reports.
  • No special hardware is needed.

How is the project creative?

  • Real units on a game meter: the radiation bar is scaled to NASA’s actual career limit, so kids see real millisieverts.
  • Each destination plays differently because of real physics: the Moon has no atmosphere and gets about twice Mars’ daily radiation, so it needs stronger shields. Mars has dust storms that weaken solar panels.
  • Real missions become game moments: MOXIE inspires the oxygen-maker upgrade, and the regolith idea comes from actual shielding research.
  • Tap-to-learn: science words open a kid-friendly explanation right where they appear.

What factors did we consider?

  • Age range: two difficulty levels, short sessions, and no violence or scary failures.
  • Plain language: jargon such as sol, regolith, microgravity and dose is explained in context.
  • Accessibility: read-aloud, large touch targets, keyboard support, reduced-motion support and high contrast.
  • Honest data: we chose a curated set of real measurements built into the game rather than live API calls. That way it works reliably for every player without API keys or outages. Every source is cited, and the data is clearly labeled as not live. Where we simplified something, the game says so; for example, radiation is sped up so one game day equals about a month.
  • Families and schools: the game supports group play, and the end screen offers discussion questions for siblings, parents and teachers.
